n1: The node’s binary question and criteria collapse the distinction between “a frog is inside” and “the requested edit is fully fulfilled.” In the edited image, one frog is visibly inside the bowl, while other frogs are on the lid and floor; the traces consistently identify the inside-bowl frog, so this is not a transport, dependency, or lack-of-evidence failure. Yet the aggregate is partial. Clarify how this node’s placement judgment contributes to the requested-change outcome, and ensure the decision criterion can represent partial progress rather than treating any visible frog inside as sufficient for completion. Do not infer that the inside-bowl frog is absent or discount it merely to match the reference: the reference constrains the aggregate, not this atomic check. Investigate whether the mismatch comes from binding the node to the whole request, an omitted completion condition, or ambiguity in how the aggregate combines checks; retain evidence-based placement judgments and avoid adding unsupported requirements.

The node’s binary question collapses the rubric’s distinction between complete and partial. In the edited image, one frog is clearly inside the bowl, while others are on the lid and floor; the traces consistently identify the bowl frog and report high confidence. Thus the observed evidence supports “complete” under the supplied criterion, not the reference “partial.” Do not force the reference label or treat extra frogs as negating the requested change. Investigate whether the criterion’s phrase “inside the toilet” is being interpreted differently from the intended placement (for example, bowl versus another toilet part), and make the node explicitly assess the rubric’s complete/partial/absent/unknown distinctions with evidence tied to the frog’s position relative to the bowl. The repeated identical yes outputs and 0.99 confidence despite aggregate disagreement indicate a criterion/binding or label-mapping ambiguity, not a transport, schema, or dependency failure; no such failures are reported. Preserve uncertainty when placement is genuinely unclear rather than inferring absence.
